Risks (assumptions): UI not verifiable without a browser (Q15); rule-variant mismatch with the requester's expectation (Q5); computer fleet leaking to the client (Q10); flaky tests from randomness (Q13); hardening of a hand-rolled static and JSON server (Q17); a sandbox refusing loopback listen (Q19); scope creep into frameworks and extras (Q2, Q12). || WHERE AND WHEN VISIBLE. The result must become usable as a project on the requester's machine: a Node server process (npm start) serving the game at http://localhost:<port>/ to a local browser. The request names this target (browser plus Node.js server), which is the grant for building and running locally; nothing is deployed, hosted or published, so no outcome exists at any remote URL, now or after the run. Timing: in an isolated run the source checkout stays at its snapshot (empty) until the final return, so the files appear there only then, and the game is playable by the requester only after that, by running npm start from the returned checkout and opening the URL. Before that the same game exists only inside the isolated workspace, observable through the run's test output and evidence. This intake stage creates no files. || INTERACTION AND STATE (answered from the request where possible, else recorded default and what it rules out). Actors: one human, anonymous with no login, plus the computer as server-side logic; a game is identified by an opaque random id, which rules out accounts and per-user history (Q8). Shared state: none across people or devices, since the request says single-player; game state is server-held, one game per id, so two tabs are two games, which rules out cross-device resume and spectators (Q8, Q9). Lifetime: server memory until the game ends, 1 hour idle expiry, or a server restart; a reload resumes via the sessionStorage id if the game still exists, which rules out persistence across restarts and any database (Q9). What ends a game: all ships of one side sunk, New game, expiry or restart. Hidden: the computer's fleet stays hidden from the browser until the game ends, and the computer learns of the player's fleet only through shot results (Q10). Already provided by the runtime (assumption): Node http, crypto, test and assert plus global fetch on the server, and DOM, fetch and sessionStorage in the browser; nothing else is installed, so no framework, bundler or database (Q12). || DISCOVERY SOURCE HINTS (leads, not verified facts). The request names no team, workspace, channel, internal site, document, private repository or owner (fact), and no sensitive locator exists, so nothing goes into KNOWLEDGE/. Owner and approver: the requester only; the run is unattended, so recorded defaults stand in for answers. || OPEN-QUESTION ROUTING. Discovery answers Q11 (Node and npm present, version), Q15 (a browser available for a smoke check) and Q19 (loopback listen and node execution permitted); every other question is answered by its recorded default, shown in questions.
